analysis.one_liner: Directs OSHA to issue voluntary advice on protecting workers from workplace violence.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with one cosponsor and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the government's job-safety research agency study workplace violence — attacks and threats against workers on the job — and then have OSHA publish voluntary advice for employers. The advice would cover things like locked doors, alarm devices, security staffing, and de-escalation training, with separate guidance for different kinds of workplaces such as hospitals, stores, and schools. Because the guidance is nonmandatory, employers could not be forced to adopt any of it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs where they face violence from customers, patients, or intruders — retail clerks, grocery and restaurant staff, hospital workers, transit and school employees. If the guidance is actually used, they get safer workplaces through better staffing, alarms, barriers, and training. But because the guidance is voluntary, the benefit depends entirely on employers choosing to act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing violence on the job

how_it_helps.text: Directs NIOSH to study how to reduce the threat of violence at work and report recommendations within 15 months.

Directs OSHA to issue voluntary guidance — tailored by workplace type from grocery stores to hospitals to schools — on engineering controls, work practice controls, and environmental risk factors that reduce workplace violence.
The guidance covers concrete protections: weapon detectors, locked doors, alarm devices, sufficient staffing, security personnel, and de-escalation training.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, employers in higher-risk industries (retail, health care, restaurants) would bear whatever cost they choose to incur in adopting the voluntary guidance — no mandates, no direct cost to taxpayers beyond the federal study.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers who voluntarily adopt the guidance

drawbacks.text: The guidance would be nonmandatory: OSHA could issue it, but no employer would be required to follow it, so the bill changes no legally enforceable protections.
The bill is slow by design — a NIOSH study within 15 months, then OSHA guidance up to 4 years after enactment — so workers would wait years for advice that employers could still ignore.

Even if adopted, the guidance favors consulting, security equipment, and staffing measures but does not itself pay for security guards, training, or equipment, leaving costs with employers and, indirectly, consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea has real merit — workplace violence is a documented hazard in retail, health care, and service jobs — but as written the bill would spend four years producing advice employers could ignore. A serious bill would make protections mandatory. The cost of the bill is minimal; the risk is that it substitutes for real action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in April 2025, never received a hearing or vote, and died there.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on April 3, 2025.
The House referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee the same day, which was its last action.
It attracted one cosponsor and never advanced to a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of workers facing violence on the job, who avoid even voluntary guidance recommendations, and status quo opponents of OSHA activity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoid even voluntary guidance

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to direct OSHA to issue workplace violence prevention guidance.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only a single Democrat cosponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan alignment is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill only asks them to consider voluntary guidance on violence prevention, imposing no requirement, though following it could mean modest spending on staffing, training, or equipment.

Health care workers face high rates of patient and visitor violence, and the bill specifically names hospitals as a workplace type the guidance must address; employers face no mandate, so the effect is informational.

industries.industry: Occupational safety and health consultants and security equipment makers
industries.note: Voluntary guidance on weapon detectors, access controls, alarms, and training could create demand for these products and services, though nothing requires anyone to buy them.

analysis.trajectory: A nonbinding guidance bill with one cosponsor and no committee action is very unlikely to advance; it would need a hearing and markup in the Education and Workforce Committee, which the Republican majority has shown no interest in scheduling.
